1. Measuring Renal Function: eGFR, Creatinine Clearance, Cystatin C

Estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) is calculated by computer from serum creatinine, age and sex; you do not need to memorize the formula. It is a surrogate for the percentage of normal kidney function. CKD stage 1 = normal GFR with evidence of kidney damage (e.g., albuminuria); stages 2–5 are defined by GFR.

eGFR ranges (slide 4): normal 90–120, early-stage disease 60–90, kidney disease 15–60, kidney failure <15.
CKD stageeGFR (mL/min/1.73 m²)Meaning
1≥90Normal GFR, but kidney damage present (e.g., albuminuria)
260–89Mildly reduced
3 (3a / 3b)30–60Mild–moderate CKD (3a/3b split is standard staging beyond source)
415–30Severe
5<15Kidney failure
Normal GFR declines with ageAverage eGFR: 20–29 y 116; 30–39 y 107; 40–49 y 99; 50–59 y 93; 60–69 y 85; 70+ y 75. Rule of thumb from the talk: about 1 point lost per year after ~65, independent of disease. CKD is usually called clinically relevant at stage 3 or worse (GFR <60).

When eGFR is unreliable

SituationWhy
Low muscle mass (elderly, cancer, anorexia, cachexia)Low creatinine production, so GFR is overestimated
High muscle mass (bodybuilders)High creatinine production, so GFR is underestimated
Rapidly changing renal functionCreatinine takes time to rise; eGFR lags. A healthy person with no kidney function rises about 1 mg/dL/day, so 3→4 in 24 h suggests essentially no filtration, while 2→2.5 means some filtration persists
Diet and creatine supplementsTransient rise in serum creatinine without true injury; creatine itself is not proven nephrotoxic

Alternatives

TestKey points
Cystatin CMade by all nucleated cells; freely filtered and reabsorbed in the tubules (inulin-like); not affected by muscle mass or diet. Not widely available, so he will not test it
Creatinine clearance (CrCl; Cockcroft–Gault)Adds body weight, so it is better when muscle mass is abnormal. Use ideal body weight in obese patients to avoid overestimating GFR. Still limited in advanced CKD, but better than eGFR. Drug dose reductions are based on CrCl, not eGFR (package inserts)

2. BUN, Azotemia and Uremia

Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) is a waste product of protein metabolism (nitrogen → urea). The kidney excretes urea, so it accumulates as function falls. Urea follows water reabsorption: in prerenal acute kidney injury (AKI) the body holds water through antidiuretic hormone (ADH) and pulls urea back with it, giving the classic BUN:creatinine >20:1. In intrinsic renal injury the ratio is closer to ~10:1.

TermDefinition
AzotemiaElevated BUN (e.g., “prerenal azotemia”)
UremiaAzotemia that is clinically relevant (signs and symptoms). Normal BUN is ~15–20; symptoms typically appear when BUN is ~100–110 or higher

How fast it changes matters: raising BUN to 70 overnight would be felt; a slow climb from 15 to 110 over two years is tolerated better.

SystemUremic manifestations
GI / nutritionAnorexia and weight loss (often first), abnormal taste (“sucking on a penny”; meat feels unappealing), nausea/vomiting
CardiopulmonaryPericardial and pleural effusions, pericarditis
HematologicPlatelet dysfunction and bleeding
Skin / nerves / brainPruritus, sensory neuropathy, cognitive dysfunction (confusion, poor concentration, encephalopathy, coma)
AKI and CKD are linkedEach AKI episode leaves the kidney slightly worse, and CKD is a risk factor for AKI. Biggest US risk factors: hypertension, diabetes, metabolic syndrome. CKD in the 20s–30s or in children makes you think genetic disease. Both AKI and CKD raise the risk of death and cardiovascular disease.

3. Interstitial Nephritis as a Cause of CKD

Usually results from chronic exposure to a causative agent. If the agent is missed (e.g., long-term beta-lactam suppression for recurrent cellulitis), exposure continues and CKD develops. It can be the presenting sign: up to 25% of biopsies for unexplained AKI show interstitial nephritis (biopsy bias: most AKI is prerenal or tubular).

Classic triad: fever, rash, eosinophilia. Urine eosinophils are no longer favored clinically, but look for them in question stems.

CauseShareExamples
Drug-induced75%Antibiotics, NSAIDs, PPIs (most common)
Autoimmune10%SLE, IgG4-related disease, ANCA-associated vasculitis, Sjögren
Infection10%—
Idiopathic5%—

The slide is titled “chronic” interstitial nephritis, but the triad and drug causes he describes are those of acute interstitial nephritis; the guide follows the slide.

4. Cystic Disease and Genetic Causes of CKD

Simple renal cysts are common and benign (typed by CT; 35% of people have >1 cyst by age 70). Isolated cysts with regular edges and no loculations are ignored. It gets interesting with many cysts.

Normal vs polycystic kidney (slide 17).
DiseaseGeneticsKey features
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD)PKD1, PKD2Most common cause of polycystic kidneys (90%); 10% of kidney failure. Hypertension 70–80%, hepatic cysts >90% over age 35, intracranial aneurysms 9–14%. ~50% need kidney replacement by ~62 y. Next best step: screen for intracranial aneurysms (coiling can save life). Imaging: kidneys replaced by innumerable cysts, plus liver cysts
Autosomal recessive PKD (ARPKD)Two gene copies neededYounger patients (e.g., a 14-year-old) with kidney cysts plus hepatic fibrosis
Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC)TSC1, TSC2 (inactivating) on chromosome 9; encode hamartin and tuberinBenign tumors of skin, brain, kidney; epilepsy, intellectual disability; kidney angiomyolipomas. Lifetime renal cell carcinoma (RCC) risk 2–3%
Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL)Autosomal dominant; VHL tumor suppressor gene, chromosome 3Tumors of eyes, cerebellum, spinal cord, adrenals, epididymis, pancreas. Pheochromocytoma in 15–30% (episodic sweating, headache, palpitations). Lifetime RCC risk 70%
ADPKD on CT (slide 18): kidneys replaced by cysts; liver cysts also visible.

Test angle: TSC is much less associated with RCC (2–3%) than VHL (70%).

Benign tumorsMalignant tumors
Renal adenoma, oncocytoma, angiomyolipoma (renal hamartoma), fibroma, lipomaRenal cell carcinoma (most common), transitional cell carcinoma, Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma; pediatric), renal sarcoma

Tumors rarely cause progressive CKD; they are usually found on imaging done to evaluate kidney disease.

5. Hematologic Complications: Anemia and Thrombosis

Anemia of CKD

The kidney’s interstitial fibroblasts make erythropoietin (EPO); with kidney loss, EPO falls and the marrow is not stimulated. Result: normocytic, normochromic anemia with an inappropriately low reticulocyte response. Often coexists with iron deficiency (uremic patients avoid red meat), so make sure patients are iron replete before starting EPO. EPO has significant side effects. He will not test anemia (covered in heme/onc).

Thrombotic tendency

Protein is lost in the urine as CKD progresses (nephrotic-type loss). The paradox: uremic platelets bleed (section 8), but the protein changes make patients prothrombotic.

ChangeEffect
Loss of antithrombin III, protein C, protein SLoss of natural anticoagulants
↑ fibrinogen, ↑ lipoprotein(a) (displaces plasminogen), ↑ platelet aggregation (the last three from low albumin)Prothrombotic

Clinical consequences: heparin is used during dialysis because clots form in the filter; increased DVT incidence. This is why not every ESRD patient is empirically anticoagulated (e.g., for atrial fibrillation) given uremic platelet dysfunction. Know only that prothrombotic complications occur.

6. Mineral and Bone Disorder: Vitamin D, Calcium, Phosphate, PTH

High-yield section: he tests through the metabolic pathways. Think “multiple hits” in every CKD problem.

Vitamin D activation

Skin/diet → liver (25-hydroxy vitamin D) → kidney proximal tubule enzyme 1α-hydroxylase → 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D (calcitriol), the hormonally active form. Loss of proximal tubule cells means loss of 1α-hydroxylase, an early event in CKD.

Regulation of renal 1α-hydroxylase (CYP1α): Ca²⁺ and 1,25(OH)₂D inhibit, PTH stimulates (slide 32).
Treatment pearlDo not supplement vitamin D2/D3 (ergocalciferol/cholecalciferol); the kidney cannot activate them, and levels of the inactive form can be normal. Give calcitriol (prescription, active form).

Hit by hit

StepMechanism
↓ CalcitriolLess 1α-hydroxylase → ↓ intestinal Ca²⁺ absorption → hypocalcemia
↑ FGF23Fibroblast growth factor 23 (bone-derived) rises early to excrete phosphate and suppresses 1α-hydroxylase, worsening the calcitriol deficit
HyperphosphatemiaFailing kidney cannot excrete phosphate. Phosphate complexes with calcium (lowers ionized Ca²⁺) and suppresses calcitriol synthesis. Ca–phos deposits calcify vessels (“PVC pipe” aorta on CT) → cardiovascular disease
Secondary hyperparathyroidismLow Ca²⁺, high phosphate, low calcitriol all stimulate PTH via the parathyroid calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR); loss of calcitriol also removes its negative feedback on PTH
PTH secretion regulated by Ca²⁺ via the CaSR; 1,25-vitamin D inhibits the PTH gene (slide 33).
Compensatory, not overshootingPTH mobilizes Ca²⁺ from bone and increases tubular reabsorption, but serum calcium stays low-normal to low, propped up by high PTH. The pathway cannot overshoot into hypercalcemia (and the failing tubules cannot respond anyway). Do not suppress PTH surgically; patients rely on it. Clinical PTH can rise from a normal of ~10–30 into the hundreds slide vs talk.
Ca²⁺ and phosphate handling along the nephron (slide 31).

Where it acts in the nephron: proximal tubule holds 1α-hydroxylase and the Na–phosphate cotransporter NPT2a (PTH normally inhibits phosphate reabsorption here); distal nephron Ca²⁺ entry through TRPV5/6 with calbindin (PTH increases distal reabsorption). He will not test these enzymes.

Bone disease of renal failure

Osteoblast RANKL drives osteoclast differentiation and bone resorption (slide 34).
MechanismResult
Continuously high PTH makes osteoblasts produce RANKL → ↑ osteoclast activityOsteitis fibrosa cystica (bone resorption)
Low vitamin DOsteomalacia
Metabolic acidosis: H⁺ buffered by bone carbonate and phosphate; stimulates osteoclast hydrolytic enzymesMore bone resorption (one reason to correct acidosis)
Long-standing diseaseOsteoporosis (more a lifelong disease than the acute CKD picture)

7. Metabolic Acidosis in CKD

The failing kidney cannot excrete the daily acid load, chiefly through reduced ammonium (NH₄⁺) excretion. Acid accumulates and consumes bicarbonate. Normally the kidney reabsorbs filtered bicarbonate and makes new bicarbonate by excreting titratable acid and ammonium; with falling nephron mass and GFR these are overwhelmed.

ConsequenceDetail
HyperkalemiaAcidemia shifts K⁺ out of cells (extracellular), and the kidney cannot excrete it. Often the driver for starting bicarbonate
Bone resorptionH⁺ buffered by bone (section 6)
When it appearsUsually CKD stage 4–5. Example: serum bicarbonate 16–18 (his lab normal 22–32) with K⁺ ~5.5–5.7

Treatment: oral bicarbonate shifts K⁺ back into cells and often fixes mild hyperkalemia. A plant-based diet lowers ammoniagenesis and acid production. Acidosis refractory to bicarbonate is a trigger to start dialysis.

8. Hyperkalemia: ECG and Acute Management

Why CKD causes it: (1) acidosis shifts K⁺ out of cells; (2) failing kidneys do not excrete it. Tolerance depends on chronicity: a CKD 4 patient living at 5.0 tolerates 5.6, whereas someone with normal kidneys at 4.0 does not. Even so, K⁺ >5.5 can cause ECG changes; peaked T waves usually appear >6.

Hyperkalemia ECG progression (slide 38).
K⁺ (mmol/L)ECG finding
6–7Peaked T waves (tall, >~50% of QRS height, pointed enough that you could not sit on it)
7–8Flattened P wave, prolonged PR, peaked T
8–9Widened QRS, ST depression, further peaking
>9Sine wave pattern; then ventricular fibrillation / pulseless electrical activity (PEA) arrest. A sine-wave patient can still be awake and talking, unlike ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation

Levels >10 are rarely from kidney disease alone (toxins, post-arrest).

Acute management: “C-BIG-K” (mostly a Step 2 topic)

LetterAgentAction
CCalciumStabilizes the cardiac membrane; does not lower K⁺. First for ECG changes; buys time
BBicarbonateAlkalinizes, shifts K⁺ into cells (works regardless of baseline bicarbonate)
IInsulinShifts K⁺ into cells
GGlucose (dextrose)Prevents hypoglycemia from the insulin; give dextrose first
KKayexalate (sodium polystyrene sulfonate)Fecal K⁺ excretion; causes severe diarrhea and bowel necrosis, so now replaced by sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (Lokelma)
AlsoAlbuterol (a few inhaled puffs), loop diuretics (furosemide)Albuterol is low risk; loops are often unhelpful with advanced renal dysfunction

For Step 1, understand why it happens (acidosis shifts K⁺ extracellularly) rather than management.

9. Complications of Uremia: Platelets and Pericarditis

Uremic platelets (bleeding)

DefectEffect
GPIb-IX-V reduced in number and functionPoor platelet binding to subendothelial von Willebrand factor (vWF)
GPIIb/IIIa (integrin αIIbβ3) abnormalPoor fibrinogen and vWF binding even after activation; excess circulating fibrinogen and fragments competitively interfere
↑ endothelial and platelet nitric oxide → ↑ platelet cGMP (and cAMP)Inhibits platelet–vessel and platelet–platelet interaction; ↓ thromboxane A₂ and ADP responsiveness
TreatmentDesmopressin (DDAVP), a synthetic ADH, releases extra vWF and factor VIII. Use for uremic bleeding (nosebleed, GI bleed) instead of platelet transfusion or clotting factors.

Uremic pericarditis

Mechanism unknown. Classic: pleuritic chest pain (better sitting forward, worse flat), pericardial friction rub (“Velcro”), fever, but in uremia chest pain is less common; a rub or unexplained hypotension during dialysis may be the first clue. Typically no diffuse ST elevation (unlike viral pericarditis). Fluid removal can transiently cause tamponade physiology. It is an indication to start dialysis; in patients already on dialysis it usually occurs within the first ~8 weeks.

10. When Does CKD Become ESRD? Starting Renal Replacement

End-stage renal disease (ESRD) means renal replacement is under way; CKD means kidneys still meet the body’s needs (uremia, electrolytes, volume). No specific eGFR or lab threshold mandates dialysis. The old “GFR <8–10” rule is gone; asymptomatic patients are monitored closely even below 10. The decision is individualized and shared (dialysis is usually lifelong).

Non-emergent triggers (uremic symptoms)Other triggers
Persistent nausea, vomiting, anorexia, metallic taste, fatigue
Pericardial rub or effusion, asterixis, altered mental status
Failure to thrive, weight loss, declining nutrition		Unresponsive hyperkalemia (diet and bicarbonate fail; potatoes matter more than bananas)
Persistent volume overload despite diuretics
Acidosis refractory to bicarbonate
Bleeding diathesis (uremic platelets)

11. Renal Replacement Therapies: HD, PD, CRRT

Modalities: intermittent (hemodialysis; sustained low-efficiency dialysis, which he will not cover again) and continuous (CRRT); also peritoneal dialysis (PD).

Hemodialysis (HD)

Typically 3 h, 3 days a week at a center. Advantages: widely used, reliable, good solute control, works in acute situations (K⁺ of 8 to ~4 in 3 h). Disadvantages: needs vascular access; bleeding and clotting issues (heparin); nutritional and fluid restrictions; hypotension and decreased perfusion that can injure remaining nephrons (midodrine is sometimes given on dialysis days); disequilibrium syndrome: rapid fall in urea and Na⁺ shifts extracellular water into cells.

Heavily tested: toxins removed by hemodialysisAspirin (ASA), lithium, ethylene glycol, methanol, isopropyl alcohol; theophylline and digoxin to some extent; antibiotics. He emphasizes lithium, methanol and aspirin for overdose questions.
HD accessNotes
Temporary catheter (neck; Trialysis)Acute dialysis
Tunneled permanent catheter (chest; placed by interventional radiology)Unplanned dialysis start; many remain on it long term
Arteriovenous fistula (vascular surgeon)Artery–vein connection in the arm; takes 6–8 weeks to mature; can thrombose. Listen for a bruit daily
GraftSynthetic fistula when vasculature is unsuitable

Peritoneal dialysis (PD)

Catheter into the peritoneum; dialysate dwells overnight and is drained in the morning, using concentration gradients across the peritoneum. Clears K⁺ and acid; less effective for volume, so volume-overloaded patients (heart failure, cirrhosis) usually use HD. More freedom (portable machine) but more patient technical skill and compliance. Peritonitis risk; repeated inflammation scars the peritoneum and makes it less permeable. In his practice ~75–80% HD, rest PD.

Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT)

Very slow dialysis, 16–24 h/day, ICU only. Preferred over HD in hemodynamic instability (on vasopressors), acute brain injury or raised intracranial pressure, and for massive volume overload (e.g., decompensated heart failure; pull 6–10 L slowly) because of small fluid shifts.

HDPDCRRT
Schedule~3 h, 3x/weekNightly, home16–24 h/day, ICU
Best forAcute solute problems, chronic ESRDPatients wanting freedom; good complianceUnstable, brain injury/raised ICP, massive volume overload
LimitsHypotension, access, disequilibriumPeritonitis, scarring, weak volume removalICU-bound, immobility

Prognosis

Survival after dialysis initiation (slide 50): ~50% at roughly 1.5–2 years.

Needing dialysis is a poor prognostic sign. About 50% survive roughly 1.5–2 years and ~20% at 5 years. Causes of death: cardiovascular disease ~50–52% (vascular calcification, inflammation), infection ~18%, dialysis withdrawal ~16%.

12. Renal Transplant

Why: better survival than dialysis despite immunosuppression risks (infection, malignancy). Graft lifespan: living donor 12–20 years, deceased donor 8–12 years. Selection bias: recipients are healthier at baseline, and still have more infections, hospitalizations and rejection risk. He will not test transplant.

Usually heterotopic (new kidney placed in the pelvis, native kidneys left in place) rather than orthotopic.

ContraindicationsDetails
AbsoluteActive cancer; active infection; unable to tolerate surgery. Hepatitis C and HIV are no longer absolute
RelativeHIV (not so much when controlled); hepatic failure (evaluate for liver–kidney transplant, e.g., hepatorenal syndrome); diabetes (consider kidney–pancreas, as almost all transplanted kidneys in diabetics show disease by 4 years; mainly type 1)

13. Medications Needing Renal Dose Adjustment

Many drugs are renally cleared; doses must be reduced as CKD progresses and especially in AKI. Test pattern: patient with AKI and a new complaint (often altered mental status) → the answer is a drug accumulating, not the infection.

DrugWhy it matters
MetforminMetformin-associated lactic acidosis. His cut-off: creatinine >1.5 contraindicated; lactate can reach mid-teens to >20 (sepsis is usually 4–6); dialysis if lactate >20. Stop the drug and give supportive care. Current labeling uses eGFR <30 beyond source
Gabapentin / pregabalinAccumulate in AKI/CKD and cause altered mental status. Example: max dose falls from 1200 mg three times daily to 100 mg three times daily in significant AKI (talk)
MorphineHepatic metabolism, but a toxic metabolite is renally excreted and causes myoclonic jerking (mimics seizures), not respiratory depression. Prefer fentanyl or hydromorphone in renal failure
LithiumRenally cleared; also dialyzable
DigoxinRenally cleared
AntibioticsMany need dose adjustment
And many moreCheck dosing references (renal adjustment is based on CrCl)
